detail:
The MedlinePlus encyclopedia describes atrial fibrillation care as built around several goals clinicians weigh together: controlling how fast the heart beats, restoring or maintaining a more normal rhythm where that is pursued, and reducing the risk of blood clots and stroke. The encyclopedia describes medicines used for rate control and rhythm control, and anticoagulant medicines, often called blood thinners, as the class used to lower clot risk, with the choice among them made by the clinician based on the person's stroke risk and bleeding risk.

The encyclopedia also describes procedures clinicians may consider, including electrical cardioversion, in which a controlled shock is used to reset the rhythm, and catheter ablation, in which small areas of heart tissue involved in the abnormal signals are treated. Management in the sources also includes treating conditions that contribute to AFib, such as high blood pressure and thyroid disorders, and follow-up monitoring of the rhythm over time, sometimes with wearable or implanted recording devices.

Tabs is not endorsing or verifying this material. Talk to your doctor about managing atrial fibrillation and heart rhythm medicines.
summary: The MedlinePlus encyclopedia describes atrial fibrillation management around rate control, rhythm control, and anticoagulant medicines for clot prevention, with cardioversion and catheter ablation among the procedures clinicians may consider.
takeaways: care centers on rate, rhythm, and clot risk, sources describe
anticoagulants are the medicine class described for stroke prevention
never start, stop, or change medicines without your doctor
title: Managing atrial fibrillation day to day
